title: Dynamic Routing and Gateway Redundancy: OSPF, EIGRP, HSRP and Troubleshooting Adjacencies
intro: Dynamic routing is the use of a routing protocol so that routers automatically exchange reachability information, build their routing tables and reroute around failures, while first-hop redundancy protocols give hosts a default gateway that survives the loss of a router. This lesson teaches how OSPF and EIGRP form neighbors and compute routes, how HSRP, VRRP and GLBP protect the gateway, and how to diagnose a stuck OSPF adjacency from show output. Static routes and basic routing-table lookup are assumed knowledge from the routing fundamentals lesson.

sections.heading: Why dynamic routing: convergence and the two protocol families
sections.content:
A router can only forward a packet if it knows a next hop for the destination. Static routes work for a stub site with one exit, but they cannot react to a failure: if a link dies, the static route keeps pointing into the hole until a human edits it. A **dynamic routing protocol** lets neighboring routers exchange information, build their tables automatically and repair them when topology changes. (How the router then picks a route from the table, longest prefix match, is covered in the routing fundamentals lesson and is not repeated here.)

The key quality metric is **convergence**: the time from a topology change until every router again holds a consistent, loop-free view. Convergence has four parts:

1. **Detection**: an interface goes down (milliseconds) or hellos stop arriving (seconds, bounded by the dead or hold timer). BFD can cut this to under a second.
2. **Propagation**: the news is flooded or advertised to other routers.
3. **Computation**: each router recomputes best paths (SPF run or DUAL).
4. **Installation**: the new best route is written to the RIB and then the FIB.

Protocols are grouped by where they run. **Interior gateway protocols** (OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, RIP) run inside one organization. **Exterior gateway protocols** (BGP) run between organizations. This lesson covers OSPF and EIGRP.

The two classic algorithm families differ in what a router knows about the network:

| Property | Distance-vector | Link-state |
|---|---|---|
| What is shared | Routes and their distance, as told by neighbors | Each router's own links and costs, flooded to everyone |
| View of topology | Second-hand: I trust what my neighbor says | First-hand: every router in the area holds the same map |
| Computation | Bellman-Ford style, incremental | Dijkstra SPF over the full map |
| Loop risk | Needs safeguards (split horizon, DUAL) | Loop-free by design inside an area |
| Resource cost | Low memory and CPU | Higher memory (database) and CPU (SPF) |
| Examples | RIP, EIGRP (advanced) | OSPF, IS-IS |

An analogy: distance-vector is asking each neighbor for directions and trusting them ("the airport is 20 minutes that way"). Link-state is every driver receiving the same road map and plotting their own route. EIGRP is usually called an advanced distance-vector or hybrid protocol because it keeps neighbor state and uses DUAL to guarantee loop freedom instead of relying on slow timers like classic RIP.

A quick way to see which protocol supplied a route is the code letter in the routing table:

```
R1# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external

C    10.1.12.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O    10.2.2.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:07, GigabitEthernet0/0
D    10.3.3.0/24 [90/3072] via 10.1.13.3, 00:02:41, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

The two numbers in brackets are administrative distance and metric, both of which matter when protocols compete, as covered later.

sections.heading: OSPF design: areas, the link-state database and SPF
sections.content:
**Open Shortest Path First** (OSPFv2, RFC 2328) is the dominant link-state IGP. Every OSPF router describes its own interfaces and neighbors in a **Link State Advertisement (LSA)** and floods it to all routers in the same area. Each router stores all LSAs in its **link-state database (LSDB)**. Within an area, every router's LSDB must be identical. Each router then runs **Dijkstra's shortest path first (SPF)** algorithm with itself as the root of the tree, producing the best path to every prefix. Two routers with the same LSDB compute consistent trees, which is why OSPF is loop-free inside an area.

**Cost** is the metric. By default the cost of an interface is reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, where the default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps. The path cost is the sum of the outgoing interface costs along the path. The classic pitfall: with the default reference, FastEthernet, GigabitEthernet and 10 GigabitEthernet all get cost 1, so OSPF cannot tell them apart. Fix it identically on every router:

```
router ospf 1
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100000
```

The value is in Mbps, so 100000 makes a 1 Gbps link cost 100 and a 10 Gbps link cost 10. Mismatched reference bandwidth across routers produces inconsistent, sometimes suboptimal paths. You can also override a single link with ip ospf cost.

**Areas** exist to limit the size of the LSDB and the scope of SPF runs. **Area 0** is the backbone, and every other area must connect to it, directly or through a virtual link. An **ABR** (area border router) has interfaces in multiple areas and summarizes between them. An **ASBR** injects routes from outside OSPF, for example redistributed static or BGP routes.

The LSA types you must recognize:

| LSA type | Name | Originated by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Router LSA | Every router | Own area |
| 2 | Network LSA | DR on multiaccess segment | Own area |
| 3 | Summary LSA | ABR | Other areas |
| 4 | ASBR summary | ABR | Other areas |
| 5 | External LSA | ASBR | Whole domain (not stub areas) |
| 7 | NSSA external | ASBR inside NSSA | NSSA, converted to type 5 by ABR |

You can inspect the database directly:

```
R1# show ip ospf database
            OSPF Router with ID (1.1.1.1) (Process ID 1)
                Router Link States (Area 0)
Link ID         ADV Router      Age   Seq#       Checksum Link count
1.1.1.1         1.1.1.1         412   0x80000007 0x00A1C4 2
2.2.2.2         2.2.2.2         398   0x80000005 0x00F3B8 3
                Net Link States (Area 0)
Link ID         ADV Router      Age   Seq#       Checksum
10.1.12.2       2.2.2.2         398   0x80000001 0x004D12
```

What matters to the analyst: the LSDB is the single source of truth. If two routers in one area disagree on a type 1 LSA, something is broken (duplicate router-id, filtering, or a flapping link). A missing advertising router in this table means that router is not adjacent to the rest of the area.

sections.heading: OSPF neighbors, DR/BDR, router-id and basic configuration
sections.content:
Before OSPF routers exchange LSAs they must become neighbors, then adjacent. They discover each other with **Hello** packets sent to multicast 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers). Two routers will form a neighbor relationship only if these hello parameters agree: the **area ID**, the **hello and dead intervals**, the **subnet and mask** on the shared link, the **authentication** type and key, the **stub-area flags**, and (for a successful database exchange) the **MTU**. Defaults are hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds on broadcast and point-to-point links, and 30 and 120 on non-broadcast types.

The neighbor state machine runs: Down, Init (I saw a hello but you did not list me yet), 2-Way (bidirectional hellos), ExStart (agree who is master for database exchange), Exchange (swap database descriptors), Loading (request missing LSAs), Full. Neighbors that sit at 2-Way as DROTHER are normal on multiaccess segments, but anything stuck at Init, ExStart or Exchange is a fault.

On a multiaccess segment such as Ethernet, forming a full mesh of adjacencies would flood redundantly, so OSPF elects a **Designated Router (DR)** and **Backup DR (BDR)**. Every other router (DROTHER) becomes fully adjacent only to the DR and BDR and sends updates to 224.0.0.6. Election is by highest interface **priority** (default 1; priority 0 means never eligible), with the highest **router-id** as tie-breaker. Election is **non-preemptive**: a new router with a higher priority does not displace a sitting DR until the DR fails or the OSPF process is cleared. On a link with only two routers, set ip ospf network point-to-point to skip the election and speed up convergence.

The **router-id** is a 32-bit identifier chosen in this order: the manually configured router-id, else the highest loopback IP, else the highest active interface IP. Always set it by hand. Two routers with the same router-id cause LSAs to overwrite each other, adjacency flaps and missing routes.

Basic single-area configuration, using the network statement:

```
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 1.1.1.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/2
```

The same result with interface-level configuration, which is more explicit and less error-prone:

```
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf 1 area 0
 ip ospf network point-to-point
```

**passive-interface** advertises the subnet but sends no hellos, which is right for user LANs. A classic mistake is making an uplink passive, which silently prevents the adjacency.

Verification:

```
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/DR         00:00:33    10.1.12.2       GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:36    10.1.12.3       GigabitEthernet0/0
4.4.4.4           1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:38    10.1.12.4       GigabitEthernet0/0
```

**OSPFv3** (RFC 5340) carries IPv6. It runs per link instead of per subnet, uses link-local addresses and multicast FF02::5 and FF02::6, and still needs a 32-bit router-id (set it manually if the router has no IPv4 address). Configuration is interface-based: ipv6 router ospf 1 globally, then ipv6 ospf 1 area 0 on each interface, or the newer router ospfv3 address-family syntax.

sections.heading: EIGRP: DUAL, successors and the composite metric
sections.content:
**EIGRP** (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol, published as informational RFC 7868) is an advanced distance-vector protocol. Instead of flooding a full map it exchanges routes with neighbors, but it keeps three tables: the **neighbor table** (adjacent routers), the **topology table** (every route learned from every neighbor) and the **routing table** (only the best). It sends hellos to 224.0.0.10 (5 seconds, hold time 15 on fast links), uses reliable transport (RTP) for updates, and sends only partial, triggered updates.

Route selection is done by **DUAL** (Diffusing Update Algorithm). Vocabulary every analyst must know:

- **Reported distance (RD)** or advertised distance: the metric a neighbor reports to reach the destination.
- **Feasible distance (FD)**: the best total metric from this router to the destination.
- **Successor**: the next hop with the lowest FD; it goes into the routing table.
- **Feasibility condition**: a neighbor is a **feasible successor** (FS, a precomputed backup) only if its RD is strictly less than the FD of the current successor. This guarantees the backup path cannot loop through us.

When the successor fails and an FS exists, EIGRP switches instantly with no recomputation. If no FS exists the route goes **Active** and the router sends queries to neighbors, which is slower and the origin of the stuck-in-active problem in large networks.

```
R1# show ip eigrp topology
P 10.2.2.0/24, 1 successors, FD is 28416
        via 10.1.12.2 (28416/28160), FastEthernet0/0
        via 10.1.13.3 (33792/25856), GigabitEthernet0/1
```

Path one has FD 28416 and RD 28160. Path two has RD 25856, which is less than 28416, so it is a feasible successor even though its total metric is worse.

The classic **composite metric** with default K values (K1 and K3 set to 1, the rest 0) is:

metric = 256 x ( 10,000,000 / lowest bandwidth in kbps + sum of delays in tens of microseconds )

For a path whose slowest link is 100 Mbps (100000 kbps, giving 100) and whose total delay is 110 microseconds (11 tens), the metric is 256 x (100 + 11) = 28416. Bandwidth is the minimum along the path, delay is cumulative, which is why tuning the delay command is the preferred way to influence EIGRP paths (changing bandwidth also affects QoS and queuing). Named mode uses 64-bit wide metrics for very fast links.

Basic configuration:

```
router eigrp 100
 eigrp router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255
 network 1.1.1.1 0.0.0.0
 passive-interface default
 no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
```

```
R1# show ip eigrp neighbors
EIGRP-IPv4 Neighbors for AS(100)
H   Address        Interface     Hold Uptime   SRTT   RTO  Q  Seq
                                 (sec)         (ms)       Cnt Num
0   10.1.12.2      Gi0/0           13 00:21:09   1    100  0  14
```

Neighbors form only if the **AS number** matches, the **K values** match, the interfaces share a subnet, and authentication agrees. An AS mismatch is silent: no error, simply no neighbor. EIGRP also supports unequal-cost load balancing with the variance command, which OSPF does not.

sections.heading: Choosing a protocol: OSPF vs EIGRP vs static, and administrative distance
sections.content:
When a router learns the same prefix from more than one source, it does not compare metrics across protocols, because an OSPF cost of 20 and an EIGRP metric of 28416 are not comparable. It compares **administrative distance (AD)**, the trustworthiness of the source. Lower wins. Only routes from the winning source are installed in the routing table, and metrics are compared only among routes from that same source.

| Route source | Default AD |
|---|---|
| Connected interface | 0 |
| Static route | 1 |
| EIGRP summary route | 5 |
| eBGP | 20 |
| EIGRP internal | 90 |
| OSPF | 110 |
| IS-IS | 115 |
| RIP | 120 |
| EIGRP external (redistributed) | 170 |
| iBGP | 200 |
| Unusable | 255 |

This explains a common surprise. If a prefix is learned by both OSPF and internal EIGRP, EIGRP (90) wins and the OSPF route stays in the OSPF database but not in the routing table. It also gives the **floating static** technique: a static route configured with an AD higher than the dynamic protocol, such as ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 10.9.9.2 130, sits unused until the dynamic route disappears.

Head-to-head comparison:

| Aspect | OSPF | EIGRP | Static |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type | Link-state | Advanced distance-vector | Manual |
| Standard | Open (RFC 2328) | Cisco-origin, informational RFC 7868 | N/A |
| Metric | Cost from bandwidth | Bandwidth plus delay (composite) | None |
| Algorithm | Dijkstra SPF | DUAL | N/A |
| Convergence | Fast, timer and SPF dependent | Very fast with feasible successor | Never self-heals |
| Load balancing | Equal cost | Equal and unequal cost (variance) | Manual |
| Scaling method | Areas | Summarization, stub routers | Not applicable |
| Multi-vendor | Yes | Mostly Cisco shops | Yes |
| Config overhead | Moderate | Low | Grows with every route |

Practical guidance:

- **Static** fits stub sites with a single exit, default routes toward an ISP, and floating backups. It scales poorly and cannot detect remote failures.
- **OSPF** fits multivendor environments, large hierarchical designs and any network where an open standard is required. Its area design requires planning but gives strong scalability.
- **EIGRP** fits Cisco-centric networks that want quick convergence, simple configuration and unequal-cost balancing.

Many real networks run one IGP internally plus static default routes at the edge, and redistribute between protocols at boundaries. Redistribution is where AD pitfalls bite: redistributed EIGRP routes get AD 170 and OSPF externals get 110, so two-way redistribution at more than one point can create routing loops unless tags or route maps are used. For a SOC analyst, an unexpected route source (for example a static route or a rogue OSPF neighbor) is a strong sign of misconfiguration or interception, so always read the code letter and AD before trusting a path.

sections.heading: The default gateway problem and HSRP
sections.content:
Hosts do not run routing protocols. A PC or server has one **default gateway** IP address configured, and every off-subnet packet goes to that address. Even if the campus has two perfectly healthy distribution routers and OSPF or EIGRP between them, the PC only knows one. If the gateway router fails, the host keeps sending frames to the dead router's MAC address, ARP entries do not help, and users lose connectivity until DHCP or an administrator changes the gateway. The default gateway is a **single point of failure** that dynamic routing cannot fix because the failure is on the host side of the router.

**First-Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRPs)** solve this by letting two or more routers share a **virtual IP address** and a **virtual MAC address**. Hosts point at the virtual IP. Whichever router currently owns it answers ARP and forwards traffic. If that router fails, another takes over the virtual IP and MAC, and hosts never change their configuration.

**HSRP** (Hot Standby Router Protocol, Cisco proprietary, described in informational RFC 2281) works like this:

- One router is **Active**: it owns the virtual IP and virtual MAC and forwards traffic.
- One router is **Standby**: it monitors the Active router and takes over when hellos stop.
- Other routers in the group sit in the Listen state.
- The group runs on a per-interface, per-group-number basis. HSRP version 1 uses virtual MAC 0000.0C07.ACxx (xx is the group number in hex) and multicast 224.0.0.2 on UDP 1985. Version 2 uses 224.0.0.102 and 0000.0C9F.Fxxx, and supports groups up to 4095 and IPv6.
- Hello is 3 seconds and hold is 10 seconds by default.

The Active router is chosen by highest **priority** (default 100, range 0 to 255), with the highest real interface IP as tie-breaker. The most common HSRP misunderstanding follows:

**Preemption is off by default.** Priority only decides who wins an election. Once a router is Active, a higher-priority router that comes online later will not take over unless **preempt** is configured on it. So R1 with priority 110 and no preempt, after a reboot, finds R2 already Active and quietly stays Standby, and the intended primary never resumes its role.

**Tracking** completes the design. If R1's uplink to the core fails but its LAN interface is fine, R1 stays Active and black-holes traffic. Interface or object tracking decrements R1's priority when the uplink drops so that R2 can preempt. The decrement must be large enough to push R1 below R2's priority, and R2 must have preempt enabled to actually take over.

Two more design points: align the HSRP Active router with the **spanning-tree root** for the same VLAN, otherwise traffic crosses the inter-switch link twice, and balance load by creating several groups (one per VLAN or subnet) with a different Active router for each.

sections.heading: HSRP configuration, verification, and comparing VRRP and GLBP
sections.content:
A typical two-router HSRP design for VLAN 10 uses real addresses 10.10.10.2 and 10.10.10.3 and virtual gateway 10.10.10.1. R1 is intended primary:

```
track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 line-protocol
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 10 ip 10.10.10.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
 standby 10 track 1 decrement 20
```

R2 gets the same virtual IP and group number, its own real address, the default priority 100 and preempt. Without preempt on R2, it would never reclaim Active when R1 degrades through tracking. Hosts use 10.10.10.1 as their gateway and never learn which router is behind it.

Verification:

```
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       10   110 P Active  local           10.10.10.3      10.10.10.1
```

Read it as: group 10, priority 110, preempt enabled (the P), I am Active, my partner 10.10.10.3 is Standby. If the Standby column reads unknown, the peer is not seen, which means a group-number mismatch, a different version (v1 and v2 do not interoperate), an access list blocking multicast, or an L2 problem. Two routers both showing Active for the same group is a classic symptom of hellos not crossing the VLAN. The command show standby on its own also reveals the virtual MAC, hello and hold timers, and the number of state changes. Frequent changes mean flapping.

HSRP is not the only FHRP. **VRRP** (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol, open standard RFC 5798) is nearly equivalent and runs on multivendor gear. **GLBP** (Gateway Load Balancing Protocol) is Cisco proprietary and addresses HSRP's weakness, that only one router forwards per group.

| Feature | HSRP | VRRP | GLBP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | Cisco (informational RFC 2281) | Open (RFC 5798) | Cisco |
| Roles | Active and Standby | Master and Backup | AVG plus up to 4 AVFs |
| Forwarders per group | One | One | Several, load balanced |
| Virtual MAC | 0000.0C07.ACxx (v1) | 0000.5E00.01xx | 0007.B400.xxyy per AVF |
| Hello multicast | 224.0.0.2 or 224.0.0.102 | 224.0.0.18, IP protocol 112 | 224.0.0.102, UDP 3222 |
| Preempt default | Off | On | Off for AVG |
| Default priority | 100 | 100 (255 for address owner) | 100 |
| Can use real IP as virtual | No | Yes | No |

GLBP's Active Virtual Gateway (AVG) answers ARP requests with different virtual MACs of the Active Virtual Forwarders (AVFs), so hosts on one VLAN are spread across routers by round-robin, weighted or host-dependent methods. Choose HSRP in Cisco-only networks, VRRP when interoperating with other vendors, and GLBP when per-host load balancing within one subnet is wanted and the extra complexity is acceptable.

sections.heading: Worked troubleshooting: an OSPF adjacency that will not reach Full
sections.content:
Scenario: you connect R1 (router-id 1.1.1.1) and R2 (router-id 2.2.2.2) over 10.1.12.0/24 in area 0, but remote prefixes never appear. Do not guess. Walk the state machine and let the state tell you where to look.

**Step 1: what state is the neighbor in?**

```
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:36    10.1.12.2       GigabitEthernet0/0
```

The state is the diagnostic. Use this decision table:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Check |
|---|---|---|
| No neighbor listed | Hellos not exchanged: passive-interface, wrong area, mismatched hello or dead timers, mask or subnet mismatch, authentication mismatch, ACL, L2 fault | show ip ospf interface, show running-config, ping the peer |
| Stuck in INIT | I hear them, they do not hear me (one-way: ACL, multicast filtering, L2 issue) | debug ip ospf hello on both sides |
| Stuck in 2WAY on a point-to-point link | Network type mismatch or priority 0 on both sides | show ip ospf interface |
| Stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE | MTU mismatch, or unicast reachability problem with large packets | MTU on both interfaces |
| Flapping Full to Down | Duplicate router-id, unstable link, dead timer too short | show ip ospf neighbor repeatedly, logs |

Here the neighbor sits in EXSTART, so basic hello parameters agreed (otherwise it would never get this far). That pattern points at **MTU mismatch**.

**Step 2: confirm on the interface.**

```
R1# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.12.1/24, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.1.12.1
  Backup Designated router (ID) 2.2.2.2, Interface address 10.1.12.2
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
  Neighbor Count is 1, Adjacent neighbor count is 0
```

The area, router-id, network type and timers are fine, and the adjacent count is 0 despite one neighbor. Now compare MTU on both routers:

```
R1# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
R2# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 1400 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
```

Confirm with a debug (use sparingly in production):

```
R1# debug ip ospf adj
OSPF-1 ADJ Gi0/0: Rcv DBD from 2.2.2.2 seq 0x1B3E opt 0x52 flag 0x7 len 32 mtu 1400 state EXSTART
OSPF-1 ADJ Gi0/0: Nbr 2.2.2.2 has smaller interface MTU
```

The mechanism: the database descriptor (DBD) packets carry each side's interface MTU. A router rejects a DBD that advertises an MTU larger than its own, so the exchange restarts forever. Hellos are small, which is why the neighbor appears at all.

**Step 3: fix.** Make the MTUs equal (preferred, since a real MTU difference also breaks large traffic). The workaround is ip ospf mtu-ignore on both ends, which hides the symptom without fixing the path.

For the other classes: a mismatched timer shows up in debug ip ospf hello as a line such as Mismatched hello parameters from 10.1.12.2 Dead R 40 C 120, Hello R 10 C 30, meaning received values versus configured values. Correct it with ip ospf hello-interval and ip ospf dead-interval, or fix the network type. A mismatched area appears as a packet received with a different area ID in the header. Always confirm the fix by seeing FULL in show ip ospf neighbor and the expected O routes in show ip route.

quiz.question: R1 and R2 share a GigabitEthernet link in area 0 with matching hello and dead timers. R1 shows the neighbor stuck in EXSTART, and R2's interface MTU is 1400 while R1's is 1500. What explains the stuck state?

options.label: The database descriptor packets advertise the interface MTU, and the larger-MTU side rejects them, so the exchange keeps restarting
The two routers have elected different Designated Routers because their priorities differ, so neither will complete the exchange
The hello packets are being dropped in one direction, so each router believes the other never saw its hello packets
The reference bandwidth differs between the routers, so their cost calculations disagree and block the database exchange

quiz.explanation: EXSTART and EXCHANGE are the database exchange phases, reached only after hello parameters already matched. DBD packets carry each side's interface MTU, and a router refuses a DBD advertising an MTU larger than its own, so the exchange restarts. A priority difference only changes who becomes DR and does not stop the exchange. One-way hello loss would leave the neighbor in INIT, not EXSTART. Reference bandwidth affects only cost values and is not part of the adjacency checks.

quiz.question: An EIGRP router has two paths to 10.2.2.0/24. The successor has FD 28416. A second neighbor reports RD 25856 with a total metric of 33792 through itself. What is the status of the second path?

options.label: It is the feasible successor, because its reported distance is below the successor's feasible distance, so it is guaranteed loop-free
It is not usable as a backup, because its total metric is higher than the successor's feasible distance
It becomes a second successor and is installed, because EIGRP always load balances across every known path automatically
It is discarded from the topology table, because only the single best path to each destination is ever stored there

quiz.explanation: The feasibility condition compares the neighbor's reported distance (25856) to the successor's FD (28416). Because 25856 is strictly lower, the path is a feasible successor even though its total metric is worse, and DUAL can switch to it instantly. Comparing total metric is the wrong test. Load balancing requires equal metrics or the variance command, and the second path does not meet that automatically. The topology table stores all feasible and non-feasible paths, not only the best.

quiz.question: R1 has HSRP priority 110 and R2 has priority 100, with no preempt configured on either. R1 reloads and R2 becomes Active. R1 finishes booting. Which router is Active afterwards?

options.label: R1 immediately, since the router with the higher priority always owns the virtual IP once it is available again
R2 stays Active, because without preempt a returning higher-priority router does not take over an existing Active router
Neither router, because both must renegotiate and the virtual IP is withdrawn until an administrator clears the group
R1 after the hold timer expires, since HSRP forces a new election every ten seconds to match priorities

quiz.explanation: Priority only decides the outcome of an election. HSRP preemption is disabled by default, so R1 joins, sees R2 already Active, and becomes Standby. Priority alone never forces a takeover. The virtual IP is not withdrawn, because R2 keeps serving it. HSRP does not hold periodic elections; the hold timer only detects a lost Active router.

quiz.question: A router learns 10.5.5.0/24 from OSPF with cost 20 and from internal EIGRP with metric 28416, and has no static route. Which statement is correct?

options.label: OSPF is installed because its numeric metric of 20 is lower than the EIGRP metric
Both routes are installed together and traffic is balanced in proportion to the two metrics
The EIGRP route is installed because its AD of 90 beats OSPF's 110, while the OSPF route stays only in its database
Neither route is installed until an administrator sets one protocol as preferred with a route map

quiz.explanation: Metrics from different protocols are not comparable, so the router compares administrative distance first. Internal EIGRP has AD 90 and OSPF has AD 110, so EIGRP wins and the OSPF route is held in the OSPF database as a standby. Comparing raw metrics across protocols is meaningless. Different sources never load balance with each other, and no manual preference is needed because default ADs already decide.

quiz.question: On a shared Ethernet segment R1 is the OSPF DR with priority 1. R3 joins later with priority 200 and a higher router-id. What happens?

options.label: R3 immediately replaces R1 as DR, because the highest priority always wins an OSPF election
R1 remains DR, since OSPF election is non-preemptive until the DR fails or the OSPF process is reset
R3 becomes DR only after the dead timer of 40 seconds has passed and R1 stops sending hellos
Both routers act as DR at once, because OSPF allows multiple designated routers on one segment

quiz.explanation: OSPF DR election is not preemptive: once a DR exists, a new router with a better priority joins as DROTHER or BDR candidate and waits. The DR changes only when the current DR fails or the process is cleared. Thinking priority always wins confuses OSPF with a preemptive election. The dead timer matters only if R1 actually stops sending hellos, and there can be only one DR per segment.
